records.query: How does Feynman develop the concept of conservation of energy across mechanics, waves and thermodynamics?
records.source_caption: 📄 Sources cited: The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Volume I  —  p. 94, p. 98, p. 155, p. 209, p. 251, p. 253, p. 277, p. 316, p. 551, p. 582, p. 804, p. 905
records.answer_head: Feynman’s treatment of energy conservation begins in the familiar setting of classical mechanics, where the simplest illustration is a body falling under gravity. He writes that the kinetic energy $T$ and the gravitational potential energy $U=mgh$ add to a constant, $T+U=\text{const}$, and that this constancy follows from the equations of motion without any appeal to a deeper mechanism (page 251).
